items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Ulver had already abandoned their black metal roots by the time they released 'Perdition City' in2000, and their previous studio release had seen them departing from their original style in favorof an experimental electronic sound that was both contemporary and haunting. But their 'Themes fromWilliam Blake' album is nowhere near as cinematic and expansive as the band's fifth studio release,conveniently subtitled 'Music to an Interior Film'. This album is perhaps the second most remarkablerecord in their discography, the first one being their unforgettably dark debut album, and whiletheir earlier releases had exhibited a dream-like gothic aura, these subsequent electronic-basedalbums are no less atmospheric and compelling. What makes 'Perdition City' even more special is thefact that this album was designed to resemble a movie soundtrack, with the premise that the musicbecomes a standalone piece rather than a collection of sounds supporting a picture.Stylistically, this is an all-out electronic album with elements of trip hop, occasional jazzypassages, swirling ambient guitars, and lots of interspersed effects, spoken word interludes,samples and noises as well as downtempo beats and rhythms. An unusual and demanding listen, thisUlver release is closer to IDM and the experimental electronic scene than it is to anything theirmetal contemporaries were producing at the time. The brooding, industrial soundscapes on some of thealbum tracks provide a haunting atmosphere that eventually evokes the feeling of being in a dark,urban setting. Undeniably this is an effective collection of electronic compositions filled withevocative instrumental passages that bridge minimalist ambient soundscapes and richly ornateelectronic grooves. Tracks like 'Lost in Moments', 'Hallways of Always', 'Tomorrow Never Knows', and'Nowhere/Catastrophe' capture the experimental inclinations of Krystoffer Rygg and Tore Ylwizaker,who are the album's primary composers, while moodier numbers like 'The Future Sound of Music' and'Dead City Centres' exhibit the uninviting urban atmosphere that this entire record highlights.Some listeners have been critical of this album throughout the years, seeing 'Perdition City' as afailed musical experiment. However, the more attentive listeners recognize it as the beginning of adelightful exploration of the avant-garde by the chameleonic project that is Ulver.

items.body: Review by agradek — I wrote this review of mine as a polemic to some reviews I read here today. Recently I forced myself to buy some outstanding CD's I missed last couple of decades; today I received the package, and... this album simply refused to get out of my player. First song starts like some of Hammil's 'singer/songwriter' albums with gentle singing on top of guitar accompaniment, and that's what I expected seeing the cover. But... do not judge the book... How many times I've already learned this lesson? At abt 2:15 I jumped from my chair at sudden hit of the bass. O-ho! there's gonna be something more in it, not just melancholically lyrical Hammill. Soon there joins rhythmic hammering of piano in the background, change of voice expression, some synth noises, sudden breaks of rhythm and tempo, and multilayered vocal lines. Then fully psychedelic last verse... No... I'm not counting the sheep, I'm not going outside, I might be right here some time. And the CD might be at home at my player's tray for quite a while!Next song taking over the mood and carries on, developing in truly haunting, multiple tangled, interfusing vocal lines... And it's only the beginning.In most psychedelically strange of the songs - "Ghosts of planes" with multiple vocal lines, we are introduced into really uneasy mood with last spoken verse, then the music carries on with tangled motives of totally weird systems music, the only con I noticed here, it does not develop further to last another 5 minutes or so.Surprisingly, I can see in some reviews, the highest note given to the simplest, "regular", standard song "Undone" - sung to rhythmic piano chords, with not many quirks in it, even with some melodic solo in the middle. I do not understand this fully, as it is Prog music portal... Even if someone may disagree the music here is "progressive", I found it interesting, engaging, hypnotizing and addictive. And I did not hear here any folk much less country music, maybe I'm deaf.In "Diminished" the lyrics end halfway into the song, and we are taken on a magical journey filled with dark and gloomy landscapes, then in the background those worrisome, scarry piano tune close to the conclusion.As a whole it's very consistent album, which simply cannot be seen as the collection of songs. One may say it's not strictly a concept-album, as there is no "developing story" or plot in it, but all songs here are bond with each other, thematically, musically and lyrically. There's no nice melodies, there's no simple riffs or familiar rhythms in it. We are haunted by disturbing or worrying sounds, dissonances, soundscapes, and hypnotized by repetitive rhythms.I could listen to this album on permanent repeat. But I cannot, as the weight of the last song and its ending is too overwhelming. I was fooled once again by the cover - though its mood is cloudy dark and blue, there's the ray of sun shining through from amongst the clouds. I was fooled by the first song, where I smelled a trace of hope in the last lines. But no. No hope here. The further we are in, the more we are assured there's none at all. Once the last song fades out, I need a good while to sort the head out, breathe in and out, rethink once again.The songs are heavy and serious; I even found them a bit depressive. Though there's no despair, there's no acceptance, either. Not yet... We experienced some kind of acceptance, even reconciling in Hammill's works in the former decades, once he seemed to grow out of his youthful fights and left behind the past letdowns with the world or people. Here, at his 51, we are facing Hammill more lost than found, again. There's uncertainty, there's insecureness, there's anxiety, maybe even fear; there's so many unanswered questions. Above all there is overbearing feeling of unreadiness. Unreadiness for irreversible loss, for disappearance. Honestly though, are we ever ready to disappear?Hammill is not the artist, who gives his listeners answers, ready solutions or recipes. He formulates the questions, sometimes directly shouting them out, often concealing them deep within verses of his involved poetries and singing them out with his unique voice, he's making the listener thinking and searching for their own responses. Same what he's been practising over the preceding forty years, he is doing in this album, with a company of some greatly enjoyable and absorbing, admirable and comprehensive music."Directionless"? Yes. Cause this is not the kind of music which proceeds in a particular direction. There's a lot of music around - from symphonies to heavy metal songs - which are running somewhere, developing, chasing something or running away, not necessarily and only at full speed, sometimes just stepping, but generally moving ahead. Music on this album just IS. Here and now. There are certain moods. Landscapes. Frameless pictures. This music is directionless. Or rather omnidirectional. It does not move. It spreads out, and while spreading it absorbs, wraps up with the sounds and keeps the listener in motionless contemplation. The only con, again, the instrumental movements could have been at least twice as long.Although my hope was to receive another Fireships, this album turned out to be completely different.And by no means worse or weaker than the mentioned one.

items.body: Review by agradek — I'm madly in anger with y'all!I do not know yet why I'm reviewing Metallica in prog-rock portal, but to be honest for me this album is the most progressive one ever made by them. Sure, it's a matter of taste, some may say it's regress, not progress, but in both cases it's a desirable way. The worst for any artist is stagnation. Freeze in place and you're dead. Try different things, step outside of the frame people put you in - you are risking losing "loyal" fans, but you go ahead, develop, stay alive. Try to experiment, do something new and unexpected - you may be sure people will be spitting at you with anger and disappointment just because they have not received what they had expected. Because people have not received, what they expected, that's why they rate this album low. Funny, but there are just two crimes here, namely:1. where are the guitar solos?2. wtf is that snare drum sound?And, as album is unlistenable, because of 1 and 2 above, there spawn immediately countless following ones: Cover. Title. Lyrics. Verses. Choruses. Vocals. Riffs. Drums. Bass lines. Length of songs. Length of the album. Inconsistency. Production ... Everything sucks!!!After a bad joke (of "S&M"), the turning-forty guys hit. And they hit with all the power. All the energy of the middle-aged men at the climax of their mental crisis. With the rawest sound ever, the album literally smashed into pieces all late 90's bull[&*!#] post-nu-sludge-stone-drone-whatverelsewannabe-metal bands.Starting with its cover, same powerfully symbolic and pregnant, like the "Kill'em All" in early 80's, and the title. What's wrong with it? The "st."? There were not once religious references in Hetfield's lyrics: "Someone help me/Oh please, God, help me", "Oh please, God, wake me", or "Pray the Lord my soul to keep". Or the "anger"? The album is filled with pure, uncontrolled anger, so why not? Then, making that anger saint, that's something! Saint, sacred, sacrosanct, untouchable.... Try to touch it, dismount and kick it out and away! Good luck!Frantic is hitting right away with raw dirty guitars separated in each channel, followed by the hated-by-all unengaged snare drum beat. Then comes the marching rhythm with interesting riff, then sudden slowdown, then back to main riff and into first verse. Melodic pre-chorus. And: "Frantic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tok! Frantic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tok! Frantic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tok! Frantic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tic, tok!", somehow bringing the memories of: "Fight fire with fire, fight fire with fire, fight fire with fire, fight fire with fire, fight!"St. AngerAfter short guitar intro, storming double feet frantic (sic!) beat suddenly taken over by melodic verses, quickly switching to next, fast and aggressive part. Several diverse parts rotate and alternate - verses, choruses, pre-choruses, pre-verses... Seven minutes of full speed rollercoaster, hold together tight with wild and heavy drumming; any shortest single guitar solo would destroy the construction of the song. The video to the song taken in San Quentin... one of the most powerful music recordings ever.I immediately bang the head against the stage, like I did before! I do not need second invitation!Sumkinda MonsterStunningly developing first two minutes of various motives, riffs, and alternating rhythms. And: "We, the People / Are we the people?". How truly true then, how [%*!#]ing truly true in 2026..."This is the voice of silence no more!" - for those who still cannot hear, feel or understand there's in the package thas bloody empty metal can snare drum. Put this empty bucket over the heads if still cannot hear!Because the angriness of "St. Anger" is different than the one of "Kill'em All", it is real. Touchable. That is what makes this album great. As much as I like the "bad" Load/Reload albums (sorry, I really do), "St. Anger" smashed me away when was released. The album is perfectly mixed. There's two guitars, drums, bass and vocals. Though noisy and dirty, everything is right here and is easily distinguishable. Does not sound like Master of Puppets? Sorry, there aren't 10 or 12 tracks of multiplied rhythm guitar for "wall of sound" effect with lead coming in to play the solo. There are 4 live musicians spitting their guts out and sweating blood through their instruments; mixed together, they sound like real, live music. The best blend of metal, hardcore and punk with some industrial. Who needs [%*!#]ing guitar solos here? Melodic parts alternating continuously with heavy rhythmic ones, unexpected changes of rhythm, tempo and mood (what some called "inconsistency") - that's what keep those songs together. And it saves the remaining pieces of brain (if any...) still rattling in the head - who would survive 75 minutes of continuous headbanging? They also make the listener to focus. To pay attention. To listen more attentively. The snare doesn't sound? That clanging sound made the record more raw, more powerful and more aggressive! A couple years ago, when "Kill'em All" was released, some more refined ears called it sounding like a chainsaw (in fast numbers) or cement mixer (in slower parts). Now you people are complaining the snare does not sound fully/beautifully enough, as "it should" sound? It's ominous... Truly.Gosh, do I need the sound I'll go to the concert hall to listen to symphony or to the opera house. I listen to Metallica now. I want noise, distortion, power, energy... And I got it! I bang the head against the stage... better than before! I'm not bitter and twisted teenager anymore. I am all but middle-aged, somewhat (I guess) schizophrenic man, who still "does not even know what the question is". But "it's my time now!" Full five stars since first listening more than 20 years ago; same five now. Last great album of Metallica is here! *_____*)= Magnetic - return to the 80's? Bull[&*!#], there's no return. That was a real "sell-out", not the "Black Album". And in fact, this direction was not what they felt they needed or wanted but was advised by a famous branding consulting company... Whoops.Everything about the Grim Reaper was said so many times already, and "we all shall die", one day. Do we need to listen this again? And why killing the sacredness? After cracker and stunning and best Unforgiven II, third one is just misunderstanding (likely written/recorded after advice from branding consultants...)= Hardwired - continuation of same direction, it could never work; Papa Het giving high fives to teenagers, it is crappy. Same sell-out. Maybe two songs worth of mentioning from 2-hour-long double album? Fail. And the cover... another full style fail. Disaster.= 72 - nothing to say about. If I'm in need of some seasons, I will look for them in the abyss, not the toddler's bed.===P.S. Someone below called up the "technical brilliance" of Ride the Lightning...From recording sessions RTL at Sweet Silence:One of sound engineers (to Rasmussen): "What's with these guys? They can't play their instruments". or:Rasmussen (asking Lars): "Why are you starting on the upbeat all the time?"Lars: "What the [%*!#] is upbeat?"That was more or less their technical brilliance at 1984. Which did not hinder them from recording one milestone cracker album.I will finish with Rasmussen answer to his colleague:"Who cares? Listen to the energy!"Five stars here, no doubts.

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — By the time Gentle Giant convened at Advision Studios in London to record their fourth album, the band already carried a reputation for making things harder than they needed to be, and had grown almost proud of it. Octopus, released in December 1972 in the UK and arriving in North America the following year, would prove the point more completely than anything they had made before. The title itself was a small private joke, coined by Phil Shulman's wife Roberta as a pun on octo opus, eight works, one for each of the record's tracks. It would also be the last album to feature all three Shulman brothers together; Phil's departure shortly afterward closed a chapter the band could never quite reopen. New drummer John Weathers, arriving in place of the previous incumbent, pushed the group toward a harder, more percussive edge than the more symphonic Three Friends had shown, without asking them to give up a single one of their contrapuntal habits. Even the cover became a small piece of divided history: Roger Dean's brooding underwater octopus for the UK pressing, and, for the American Columbia edition, a die cut jar containing the creature, illustrated by Charles White, an alternate icon progheads still argue over four decades later.Musically this is Gentle Giant distilling everything they had been reaching toward since Acquiring the Taste into its most confident form yet. The band's love of counterpoint and layered polyphony is everywhere, five multi instrumentalists trading violin, cello, saxophone, vibraphone, and recorder as easily as most bands trade verses, yet the record never collapses under its own cleverness; there is a real, earthy humor running beneath the complexity, something closer to a traveling troupe of jesters than to a conservatory recital. The literary sources are worn openly and without pretension: The Advent of Panurge borrows its giant and his companion from Rabelais, A Cry for Everyone leans on Camus, and Knots takes its very structure from R. D. Laing's book of the same name, its tangled a cappella lines mimicking the knotted patterns of family communication the psychiatrist had described. Ray Shulman himself would later call this, alongside Acquiring the Taste, the best record the band ever made, and it is hard, listening today, to disagree; few groups of the era managed to sound so serious and so unserious about themselves in the very same bar of music.The album unfolds across eight pieces that, however different in temperament, all seem to share the same restless intelligence:- The Advent of Panurge opens the record at full throttle, Gary Green's guitar cutting in short, jagged bursts over a thundering bass and the occasional churchy organ swell, Rabelais's giant meeting his lifelong companion in music as boisterous as the text itself.- Raconteur, Troubadour turns toward a more medieval, violin led lyricism, the closest the band comes here to something like a chivalric ballad.- A Cry for Everyone digs into a heavier, almost bluesy groove, its philosophical unease wrapped in one of the album's most straightforwardly rocking arrangements.- Knots stands as the record's great vocal experiment, its interlocking, sometimes atonal a cappella patterns drawn directly from Laing's psychiatry, punctuated by a xylophone solo from Weathers that has become one of the band's signature moments.- The Boys in the Band shifts into pure instrumental territory, high intensity and almost orchestral in its arrangement, a portrait, fittingly, of the group itself at full stretch.- Dog's Life lightens the mood considerably, a warm, medieval tinged piece written with evident affection for the band's own touring roadies.- Think of Me with Kindness slows everything down into something gentle and nearly majestic, and stands, in hindsight, as Phil Shulman's quiet farewell to the band he was about to leave.- River closes the record on more familiar blues rock ground, its extended guitar and violin interplay recalling the band's earlier, less ornate beginnings, a calmer tide after seven tracks of turbulence.Heard in full, Octopus remains one of those rare progressive records that asks a great deal of patience from its listener and repays every last bit of it, a genuinely inventive, endlessly rewarding piece of work that only reveals the full extent of its craft after many returns to the same eight tracks. What might elsewhere read as restless variety here holds together as something closer to a single, many chambered organism, each piece feeding naturally into the next until the whole record breathes as one. Very few bands of the era managed to sound this serious and this playful in the very same breath, and fewer still left behind a record so entirely without a weak moment. This is Gentle Giant at its absolute peak, and a genuine landmark of the entire progressive rock canon.Rating: 5/5

items.body: Review by Stefano61 — By the time Jumbo entered the rehearsal room on via Benadir in Milan, a hall once used for Fascist era press briefings, the band led by singer and songwriter Alvaro Fella had already burned through a tentative solo styled debut and the far more accomplished DNA. What they built there in barely two weeks would become something else entirely: a record so direct in its subject matter, so unwilling to soften itself for polite radio play, that the question mark in its title reads less like uncertainty than like a dare. Vietato ai minori di 18 anni translates plainly as Forbidden to minors of 18 years, and Fella, who wrote every lyric himself, filled it with the era's unspoken subjects: drug addiction, prostitution, alcoholism, social marginalization, a crisis of religious faith, even a frank and sympathetic look at homosexuality at a time when Italian state broadcasting simply refused to acknowledge such things existed. The result was total silence from RAI, the only network that mattered then; almost nothing from the album was ever aired, and the band's boldest gesture became, commercially, its own punishment. And yet the record found its audience anyway, through years of relentless live performance, and today stands as the closing statement of a group that never got the recognition its ambition deserved.Musically this is Jumbo at its most confident and least indebted to any single foreign model. Where earlier records leaned on recognizable English touchstones, here the band forges something harder to place: folk passages give way without warning to raw, almost punishing hard rock, then just as suddenly to passages of near classical piano restraint. New drummer Tullio Granatello, arriving with a more jazz inflected touch than his predecessor, pushes the rhythmic complexity considerably further than DNA had attempted. Fella's voice remains the record's central instrument, a rasping, theatrical, at times genuinely harsh sound that some listeners need time to accept and that others count among the finest in all of Italian prog. Around him, guitarist Daniele Bianchini contributes stretches of genuinely intense playing, at points recalling the ferocity of Il Balletto di Bronzo's Ys, while contributions from two figures of the Italian avant garde, Franco Battiato on synthesizer oscillators and Lino Capra Vaccina on percussion and bells, add a genuinely experimental edge that few of the band's peers would have risked.The album unfolds across eight pieces that move from confrontation to something close to confession:- Specchio opens the record already at full tension, its shifting meters and searing guitar work eventually giving way to an unexpected softness carried by violin, as though the mirror of the title had caught something the band could not immediately look away from.- Come vorrei essere uguale a te follows, the album's emotional core and, tellingly, its only track ever granted the occasional radio spin, a plea built around difference and the wish to belong that carries far more tenderness than its taboo subject matter might suggest.- Il ritorno del signor K passes almost as a brief, unsettled interlude, barely two minutes long, a shadow crossing the record rather than a fully inhabited song.- Via larga continues in a restless vein, shifting between the band's folk instincts and its harder edges without settling comfortably into either.- Gil moves along a similar path, its identity harder to pin down than the surrounding tracks, content to remain one more shifting scene in a record built entirely from contrasts.- Vangelo? poses its title as a genuine question, religious certainty examined and found wanting.- 40 gradi burns with a feverish intensity that its title only half explains.- No! closes the record as pure, unapologetic defiance, a young generation's refusal of bourgeois convention delivered with some of the album's finest keyboard work and a vocal performance from Fella that holds nothing back, the last word of a band that clearly meant every one of them.Heard today, Vietato ai minori di 18 anni still carries the charge of a record that refused every easy compromise available to it, and paid for that refusal almost immediately. It is not a flawless album, certain passages ask more patience than others, but its ambition, its honesty, and the sheer conviction of its performances place it comfortably among the strongest statements Italian progressive rock produced in its golden years.Rating: 4/5

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 977Brand X is a British progressive rock band that was founded in London in 1975. Brand X was a jazz fusion band that was active between 1975 and 1980 and had a hiatus from 1980 to 1992. The band was disbanded in 1999 and was reformed in 2016. Brand X is one of the best, most original and well known British bands in the 70's of the jazz rock fusion scene. Brand X started in 1975 as a "jam" band funded by the Island Records to keep track of their activity on the studio schedule. The original drummer and vocalist Phil Spinelli and the guitarist Pete Bonas departed the band after recording the first and disappeared/unreleased Brand X album. Genesis' drummer Phil Collins took over on drums and, in the early of 1976, their debut album "Unorthodox Behavior" was released to coincide with an extensive UK live tour.Brand X released four studio albums in the 70's. Their debut studio album "Unorthodox Behaviour" was released in 1976. Their debut live album "Livestock" and their second studio album "Moroccan Roll" were both released in 1977. Their third studio album "Masques" was released in 1978. Their fourth studio album "Product" was released in 1979.So, "Unorthodox Behaviour" is the debut studio album of Brand X that was released in 1976. The line up on the album is John Goodsall (electric, acoustic and 12-string acoustic guitars), Robin Lumley (piano, Fender Rhodes electric piano and Moog synthesizer), Percy Jones (fretless bass, marimba and acoustic bass) and Phil Collins (drums, percussion, tambourine and vibes). The album had also the participation of Jack Lancaster (soprano saxophone), as guest.In 1975 the city of London was the perfect melting pot to generate music of a stratospheric level and even in all that decade. And although punk was already beginning to show its weariness towards the usual proposals at the time, Brand X offered us their unorthodox vision. "Unorthodox Behaviour" was an album of smooth, elegant, soulful and all instrumental jazz rock, totally different from the kind of jazz rock that was being offered by the Canterbury school of progressive rock. This is jazz rock in the direction of Mahavishnu Orchestra, Return To Forever or Weather Report, but there are also allusions to the classic prog. Musically, it's at the very highest level. The album displayed amazing group improvisation and counterpoint. The album is a fusion of rock and jazz. "Unorthodox Behaviour" covers a variety of styles from melodic to energetic, and ethereal to mathematical. It's punctuated by the distinctive characteristic playing of Jones and Collins balanced by the frenetic guitar work of Goodsall and the stylistic synthesis of Lumley. But, the pillars on the album are the two members of the rhythm section. The bass and drums have the most distinctive sounds."Nuclear Burn" is an amazing opener where Collins and Jones erupt in unison. Phil and Lumley enter to introduce us to the song and Goodsall who, together with Lumley, exudes a wonderful solo. The 70's jazz fusion flavour is perfectly audible. "Euthanasia Waltz" is much calmer. It follows the repertoire with a melodious and dynamic piece that finds Goodsall playing captivatingly and where the acoustic guitar is the dominant instrument. Collins and Jones' cuts are stunningly precise. "Born Ugly" is a groovy number where the band shares a bit of funk without getting too far apart. It can be best described as an improvisation session with a structure. The middle part is a bit psych as the band weaves large soundscapes with growing intensity. "Smacks Of Euphoric Hysteria" is probably the least euphoric song in the all repertoire, but it's highly attractive too. It has a slow groove. There's an obvious intention to give each musician the same time in the centre spot but Phil's drums are really in the front. The title track is another piece that sounds like an improvised jam. It begins quiet and even hesitating and builds up a tension that it's broken up suddenly by Phil's drumming. A dialogue develops between the guitar and the keyboards and where bass and drums occasionally pop in. "Running On Three" is a piece where the band makes a rhythmic melodic experience. It's a fast track where bass and drums play intriguing roles. Keyboards share the melodic work with a guitar solo of rock in the middle. The overall impression is a jazz jam. "Touch Wood" closes this great debut with delicacy where Lancaster's nuances with his soprano saxophone, the Goodsall's acoustic guitar and Lumley's keyboards, fill us with warmth, especially at the end.Conclusion: "Unorthodox Behavior" is a very well done instrumental debut album. You can feel that the musicians are very much in tune with each other. There are plenty of excellent instrumental parts here. It seems that all tracks were developed from jam sessions and structured later. You can hear typical jam-heavy fusion here, based on rather short carrying riffs or licks. The songs have less of a fixed structure that is then easy to follow. We can say that Brand X is definitely more for jazz rock fans than for the traditional progressive rock fans. So, if you like your 70's jazz fusion with catchy hooks and complex rhythms you will adore Brand X's "Unorthodox Behaviour". It certainly set the tone for the band's subsequent releases. But this is the album that showcases them at the peak of their humour and "innocence".Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by UMUR — "Pictures From Cyclus 7" is the third full-length studio album by Danish progressive rock act Ache.The album was released through CBS Records in May 1976. It�s the successor to "Green Man" from June1971. There have been quite a few lineup changes since "Green Man" and only guitarist Finn Olafssonand keyboard player/backing vocalist Peter Mellin remain from the lineup who recorded thepredecessor. New in the lineup are Stig Kreutzfeldt (vocals, percussion), Johnnie Gellett (vocals,percussion, guitars), Steen Toft Andersen (bass), and Gert Smedegaard (drums).Probably as a result of the changes in musical winds since 1971 and the major lineup changes takingplace, "Pictures From Cyclus 7" almost sounds like a completely different band to the Ache whorecorded and released "De Homine Urbano" (1970) and "Green Man" (1971), which were both organ heavyprogressive rock albums rooted in late 60s psychedelic blues rock but with a sophisticated touchincluding classical music and jazz-rock elements. "Pictures From Cyclus 7" instead sounds like amore progressive inclined Supertramp. The addition of several new vocalist to the lineup hasprovided Ache with more options and as a result "Pictures From Cyclus 7" features a lot of vocalparts, harmony- and backing vocals, and choirs, and they are very well performed. Ache are arguably still on an international level when it comes to the quality of their songwritingand the performances. Add to that a well sounding production job, and "Pictures From Cyclus 7" isoverall a high quality release. It may not appeal to fans of the first two albums, but fans of themore polished and AOR leaning progressive rock albums of the mid- to late 1970s (artists like Saga,Queen, Supertramp, Electric Light Orchestra, and 10cc) will probably find a lot to appreciate here.A 3.5 star (70%) rating is deserved.

items.body: Review by Matti — If the 2-CD compilation Prog Rock and Beyond (that I reviewed a few days back) was an example of a poorly done Various Artists set, here we have a total opposite. Esoteric Recordings, namely Mark Powell, has a long experience in re-releasing vintage prog albums with careful and informative liner notes. In addition to the artist-based, expanded re-releases, Esoteric has put out conceptual V. A. box sets, and progressing year by year is one of those concepts. This 4-disc set concentrates on the year 1973, which still was a very good prog year.Instead of going through the selection with a massive amount of name dropping (you can form the picture of the musical contents yourself simply by reading the track list), I will concentrate on pros and cons of the whole. The outlook, the layout, all of that, is excellent. What I was missing again were the tracks lengths, but happily they were to be found on Discogs. The 60-page booklet is very user-friendly. After the track credits comes Powell's brief and up-to-the-point essay on the state and status of prog in 1973, dealing with the album format vs. single, the music media, the prog oriented record labels. After that comes the artist by artist liner notes, in alphabetical order, offering a basic but thorough career-spanning information of each included artist/band. This approach is fairly wise, especially serving well those listeners who are not yet advanced connoisseurs of the genre. The negative side of it is that the texts are a bit dry and always more or less the same from compilation to compilation, as they don't really speak of the track choices themselves (which approach I have appreciated on numerous V. A. sets released by other labels).For a connoisseur these Esoteric box sets are actually rather predictable, especially if you have paid attention to which prog (related) bands they have been re-releasing over the years. Borderline surprises are few and easily acceotable, such as AL STEWART or JOHN MARTYN. Surely the set is missing even some big names such as Genesis, Jethro Tull, King Crimson and Mike Oldfield, and the list of potential artists with releases from the year 1973 would ubdoubtedly be long. In that respect, I wonder a little why several source albums are visited twice in this set (by e.g. Camel, Caravan, Kevin Ayers, Arthur Brown's Kingdome Come, Spirogyra and Pete Sinfield). All artists are British except PFM whose English-language albums were released by ELP's own Manticore label.Bands that I wasn't very aware of included HEMLOCK, PINK FAIRIES and STRAY. A delightful surprise was ANTHONY PHILLIPS whose 1973 'Silver Song' - - featuring Mike Rutherford as co-composer and Phil Collins on vocals - - has been released in an archival setting. It also must be said that there are plenty of tracks exceding the ten minute length. And what could be a more gorgeous closing piece than RENAISSANCE'S 'Ashes Are Burning'.

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — With this new LP, released just yesterday, Hesse Kassel has settled, most likely permanently, theirmusical identity, aesthetical approach and most importantly, their brand, ever since the release of"La brea" in February 2025, the band has just grown larger and larger within not only the Chileanindie scene, but the international as well. They've been awarded the Pulsar award for "Best newband", have been reviewed and displayed in several magazines worldwide and have even madecontroversial statements about politics which have drawn even more attention to them, it's naturalthat now the band has a dedicated cult following.Following the release of their single "Sancho plagio" during late April 2026, a part of me wasafraid that they would"sell out", boy as I wrong! That was their only single for this LP, andalthough it foretold the direction they would take, the left turn still felt sudden, butrecognizable, a big feat for a relatively new band.It's also worth noting and admiring just how quickly they were able to compose, play, produce andrelease new material...their schedule has been bloody busy, touring, college, rehearsals...and yet,they were able to put a record in less than a year and a half, this speaks wonderfully about thecapabilities of the members.And to finish of this introduction, it's also worth noting that frontman Renatto Olivares, hadrecently also released his solo EP "Aguas raras" which takes an interesting approach of traditionalfolk music mixed with post rock and spoken word poetry, it's a high quality record I'd alsorecommend checking out, preferably before listening to the record I'll review ("Morir saltando") nowas it highlights how insanely creative and efficient the boys are, and also highlights how they arenot afraid of making huge left turns while keeping their identity intact.The first aspect I'd like to analyse, are the compositions. Parallel to their previous release, thefirst track sets the tone immediately and is not afraid to violently take you inside the aura of therecord...what's the difference? "La brea" takes a more melodical, jazzy and math rock approach,while this record immediately throws you to an aggressive, ritmical, industrial, Avant Gardelandscape. The compositions are intricate, complex and noisy, they have expanded more on thisinfluence they have addressed on interviews, the main characters will be Matthew and Eduardo withtheir bass guitar and drums, the bass is overdriven, loud, aggressive and has the attack of a wolfready to hunt down it's prey, the drums are strident like an artillery regiment, complex and yet,delicate, in the way thunders are. The main feat the composition have is their dramatism,crescendos, loud sections, sudden halts and aggressive come backs, industrial noises, atonality andaggressiveness are present throughout all the album, even on the "tamer" more melodic pieces such as"El reflejo" and "Tulpa", they are not afraid to be uncomfortable and daring, Renatto shouts a lot,and instead of delicate pianos like in la Brea, we have moody synth backgrounds. The album soundslike a mix of post-punk, industrial, noise and Avant jazz, at times it feels like Coltrane's"Meditations", if that doesn't say "high quality", I don't know what will. Creativity withaggression, engaging uncomfortableness, dramatic without being overly bloated.The production is also very clean, it highlights the clean sections very well and captures eachinstrument individually and crystal clear, that's amazing for a noise album...the musicianship isalso quite strong, and Renatto sings much better than in previous releases!The lyrics are of social critique and political protest, ir highlight "Profesan tu tierra y la horcate ponen" ("They profess your nation and then will hang you"), this goes hand in hand with theaggressive tone of the album...This album is delightful, it's a must listen... seriously, do so, you won't regret it

As always, you can rate and subscribe on iTunes, download directly, or listen through the widget down below. The post We Have A Technical 618: Vodka Colonic? appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: San Francisco minimal synth duo Frozen Warnings released an official video for “Locked Out” on 11 July 2026, directed by Fred Joseph. The same day, the band made available the “Locked Out Remixes EP,” a four-track companion release issued 10 July 2026 through God’s Eye Records. “Locked Out” itself originally appeared on the duo’s album “Momentum,” released 7 February 2026. Frozen Warnings are Walker Phillips and Caira Paravel, who share vocals and production. “Locked Out” pairs a drum machine, a cold bass line and a chanted vocal loop. The band described the song’s origin: “Locked Out was written spontaneously during rehearsal when the studio computer locked itself, Caira began chanting ‘locked out!’ and I joined in, sampling my voice as the arrhythmic loop that forms the song’s core texture. The rest was improvised quickly to keep the spirit. On the Locked Out Remixes EP, we explored more deliberate remix arrangements.” Frozen Warnings’ ‘Locked Out Remixes EP’ adds single edit, remix and live versions The “Locked Out Remixes EP” gathers four versions of the track: “Locked Out – Single Edit,” “Locked Out – Smash The Lock,” “Locked Out – Aliaser Remix” featuring Aliaser, and “Locked Out – Live.” The EP runs 14 minutes and 27 seconds and is credited to God’s Eye Records. On the video, shot on VHS-style footage by director Fred Joseph, the band commented: “The video was heavily processed by director Fred Joseph with vintage equipment, filming off of screens and that kind of thing. It was shot very spur of the moment, mirroring the approach we took to recording the song – basically, using old technology and letting chance take over.” Locked Out by Frozen Warnings “Locked Out” streams on Bandcamp; the “Locked Out Remixes EP” streams on Spotify. No physical format has been confirmed for either release. About Frozen Warnings Frozen Warnings is the San Francisco duo of Walker Phillips and Caira Paravel, who share vocals and production across minimal synth, punk and industrial material. The band describes its outlook in a manifesto: “We have no history that is meaningful, we only look forward and abandon hope with total optimism. Dance is the eternal now, in dance we destroy our past and our future.” The duo self-released the two-track EP “Provider” on 17 January 2025, followed by the ten-track album “Momentum” on 7 February 2026, which included “Locked Out” as its fifth song. “Locked Out” returned in July 2026 with an official video and the “Locked Out Remixes EP,” the band’s first release through God’s Eye Records.

items.body: Seattle synthwave duo Dead Astronauts released the single “Get Lost” on Bandcamp on 26 June 2026 via Cold Transmission Music, and followed it on 10 July 2026 with an official video. “Get Lost” is the first single from the band’s forthcoming fifth studio album, “Shallow Grave.” No release date for the album has been announced. “Get Lost” layers synthesizer, guitar and processed atmosphere under vocals from Jared Kyle over a steady electronic rhythm. The lyrics follow a relationship described in terms of consumption and erasure, repeating the line “what will you do when I’m just bones” across the verses. The song and its video are credited to the duo of Kyle and Slade Templeton. Get Lost by Dead Astronauts Dead Astronauts’ video for ‘Get Lost’ shows masked figures around Jared Kyle The video for “Get Lost” was shot on degraded, VHS-style footage and shows masked figures gathering around Kyle as hands reach toward him. No director has been credited for the clip. “Get Lost” streams on Bandcamp. No further platform availability has been confirmed for the single. About Dead Astronauts Dead Astronauts began in Seattle in 2011 as a synthpop project and digital art initiative founded by designer and producer Jared Kyle Nickerson. Hayley Stewart of Toronto joined in 2012 as producer, vocalist and lyricist, and the expanded lineup released the debut album “Constellations” in 2014, followed by “Arms of Night” in 2016. In early 2017, Slade Templeton, previously of Crying Vessel and Celine, joined as producer. The band moved to Cold Transmission Music around 2020, starting with the single “Forgetting Me.” Florence Bullock of Los Angeles joined on vocals and lyrics the same year. Cold Transmission Music released “Silhouettes” in 2021, reissued the following year as “Silhouettes Redux,” and released the album ‘Ghosts’ in 2024. The band self-released the collaborative single “Yuu Yuu” in December 2025. “Get Lost,” released in June 2026, opens the campaign for Dead Astronauts’ fifth studio album, “Shallow Grave,” with Kyle and Templeton fronting the release.

items.body: Oráculo Records has opened preorders for “Burning The Edges”, the new 12″ vinyl release from Hungarian duo Post Analog Disorder. The label is pressing the record in a one-off edition of 300 lacquer-cut copies on 180 gram solid black vinyl, with shipping expected around 25 September to 5 October 2026. Burning The Edges by Post Analog Disorder Post Analog Disorder mixes EBM, hard-beat techno and post-punk, combining analogue basslines, sequencer lines, female vocals and guitar parts. Oráculo Records describes the record as moving “between industrial ritual, post-punk melancholy and […] electronic experimentation,” built for “the darkest dancefloors” as well as listeners drawn to less conventional corners of underground electronic music. The individual band members and the vocalist featured on the release have not been publicly credited. All tracks on “Burning The Edges” were remastered for vinyl by Daniel Hallhuber at Young and Cold Studios in Germany. The release is distributed through Oráculo Records (Spain) and Bordello A Parigi. Post Analog Disorder’s ‘Burning The Edges’ ships as a 300-copy vinyl pressing The 12″ comes as a single pressing run rather than a reissue-ready edition: once the 300 copies are gone, Oráculo Records has not indicated plans for a repress. The preorder window covers the period before the September-October 2026 shipping estimate; no digital or streaming release date for “Burning The Edges” has been confirmed alongside the vinyl. The preorder is one of four Oráculo Records vinyl releases opened this week, alongside Estado De Bienestar’s “Capítulo IV”, IP307’s “IP307.1” and Frontmaschine’s “Rühren.” About Post Analog Disorder Post Analog Disorder is a Hungarian project that formed in the early 2020s, mixes post-punk, darkwave, EBM and synthpop. The duo has released a run of albums, EPs and singles through Bandcamp, including the 2024 album “The Echoes Of The Past,” issued on CD in Hungary on 4 April 2024 in the darkwave and EBM styles, alongside titles such as “Live For Today,” “Silent Shout” and “Start Over.” “Burning The Edges” marks the project’s new vinyl release through Oráculo Records. No individual member names or a formal biography have been independently confirmed beyond the project’s own Bandcamp description of its sound and origins.

items.body: IP307, the project of Israel Padilla, has opened preorders for a new 12″ EP titled “IP307.1”, set for release through Oráculo Records. The Spanish label is pressing the six-track record as a one-off limited edition of 300 copies on 180-gram solid black vinyl, with copies expected to ship between 25 September and 5 October 2026. IP307.1 by IP307 Oráculo Records describes the material as blending “the most dub-infused and mechanical forms of electro with industrial, EBM and even post-punk,” calling the result “hypnotic, forceful and deeply cathartic.” The label states the EP consists of six interconnected compositions, each with its own identity while contributing to what it describes as a coherent vision built from otherwise opposing styles. Behind IP307 is Israel Padilla, who founded Banshees Records, a Toledo, Spain-based label established in 2021 and focused on dark disco, slow techno, EBM, industrial and Italo sound. Padilla has also released solo material on that label under his own name, including 2021’s “Apertura Industrial.” Oráculo Records describes IP307 as building on the later-period work of Clock DVA and on Atom™, both through Padilla’s solo output and, according to the label, as part of ASA alongside Esplendor Geométrico. Side-Line could not independently verify Padilla’s involvement in ASA: published credits for ASA’s 2023/2024 album “Radial,” released on the Raster label, list Atom™ (Uwe Schmidt) and Esplendor Geométrico (Arturo Lanz and Saverio Evangelista) as the project’s members, with no reference to Padilla found in Discogs, Bandcamp or label listings for that release. All six tracks on “IP307.1” have been remastered and mastered for vinyl by Daniel Hallhuber at Young and Cold Studios in Germany. Oráculo Records positions the release alongside recent additions to its catalog, including Mystic Letter K’s “Occulimus,” released in March 2026, and material by Maman Küsters, describing all three as part of what it calls an emerging strand of dark electro. ‘IP307.1’ ships as a 300-copy vinyl preorder through Oráculo Records “IP307.1″ is not yet shipping; it is currently available to preorder, with Oráculo Records and its distribution partner Bordello A Parigi listed as the release’s outlets. The label has not published a tracklist beyond stating the EP runs six tracks, and no additional formats beyond the black vinyl 12” have been announced. The preorder is one of four Oráculo Records vinyl releases opened this week, alongside Estado De Bienestar’s “Capítulo IV”, Frontmaschine’s “Rühren” and Post Analog Disorder’s “Burning The Edges.” About IP307 IP307 is a project of Israel Padilla, who also founded and runs Banshees Records, an EBM, industrial, dark disco, slow techno and Italo label based in Toledo, Spain, that launched in 2021. Under his own name, Padilla has released material on Banshees Records including “Apertura Industrial” and “Los Intrusos.” Oráculo Records, the Spanish label issuing “IP307.1,” was founded by Nico Cabañas and Vanessa Asbert in 2014 and specializes in limited-edition darkwave and electro vinyl; its recent catalog includes Mystic Letter K’s “Occulimus” and releases by Maman Küsters. Side-Line found no prior release credited to the IP307 name on Discogs, Bandcamp or elsewhere, which is consistent with “IP307.1” being the project’s first outing, though this could not be conclusively confirmed. The label’s description of Padilla as a member of ASA, the collaborative project otherwise credited to Atom™ and Esplendor Geométrico, could also not be independently verified.

items.body: Oráculo Records has opened preorders for a limited vinyl edition of Frontmaschine’s “Rühren”, pressed with Bordello A Parigi in an edition of 300 copies on 180 gram solid white vinyl. Shipping is expected between 25 September and 5 October 2026. Frontmaschine is the French father-and-son EBM duo of Hervé and Louis. “Rühren” first appeared digitally on 29 May 2025 as a 13-track album through the duo’s own Bandcamp page, and the new 12″ brings the material to vinyl for the first time. Oráculo Records describes the record as built around “cold, almost chilling polyphonic synthesizer melodies” intertwined with drum programming the label places “somewhere between the militant precision of DAF and the mechanical drive of the ‘Commando days’ of Front 242.” RÜHREN by FRONTMASCHINE All tracks for the vinyl pressing have been remastered by Daniel Hallhuber at Young and Cold Studios in Germany, the same mastering engineer and studio credited on the duo’s earlier “Wrong Fate” EP. Frontmaschine’s ‘Rühren’ pressed as a one-off white vinyl edition The 12″ is described by the label as a one-off, truly limited pressing rather than an open or repeatable edition. No exact tracklist for the vinyl cut has been published alongside the preorder announcement, and Side-Line could not independently confirm whether it carries the full digital tracklist or a selection of it. The preorder is one of four Oráculo Records vinyl releases opened this week, alongside Estado De Bienestar’s “Capítulo IV”, IP307’s “IP307.1” and Post Analog Disorder’s “Burning The Edges.” About Frontmaschine Frontmaschine is a French project formed by Hervé and Louis, a father-and-son duo who build tracks around synthesizer sequences, programmed drums and samples in the tradition of early body music. Full surnames and an exact founding date could not be independently verified. The duo’s first release, the digital EP “Los geht’s”, came out on 6 October 2020 through their own Bandcamp page. Later that year, the 12″ EP “Wrong Fate” followed as a limited edition of 200 copies on 180 gram solid red vinyl, issued jointly by Oráculo Records and Bordello A Parigi and mastered by Daniel Hallhuber at Young and Cold Studios in Germany. Frontmaschine’s next full body of work, “Rühren”, was released digitally as a 13-track album on 29 May 2025 through the band’s own Bandcamp page. The new Oráculo Records and Bordello A Parigi 12″ edition brings that album to vinyl for the first time, marking the duo’s second physical release on the label after “Wrong Fate”.

items.body: Estado De Bienestar has opened preorders for “Capítulo IV: La Fiesta Seria y Nuevas Formas de Tecnaco”, the fourth chapter in the project’s ongoing series, through Oráculo Records. The Spanish label and Bordello A Parigi are handling distribution for the release, a one-off limited edition of 300 copies pressed on 180 gram solid black vinyl across two 12″ records. Shipping is expected between 25 September and 5 October 2026. Capítulo IV: La Fiesta Seria y Nuevas Formas de Tecnaco by Estado De Bienestar Across the album, Estado De Bienestar moves between tribal dub, primitive electro, hypnotic ambient passages and classical piano structures. Most of the material was built from CV sequences driving synthesizers from different generations, and the album was recorded almost entirely in analog, keeping the lo-fi character that has run through the project since its debut. Oráculo Records, which has previously described the project’s sound as one that some international specialist outlets called “a new genre because of its unclassifiable nature,” refers to this direction internally as Transelectronica. All tracks on “Capítulo IV” were remastered and mastered for vinyl by Daniel Hallhuber at Young and Cold Studios in Germany, the same mastering engineer who worked on the project’s prior releases. Estado De Bienestar’s ‘Capítulo IV’ follows ‘Capítulo III: La Anarquía Sónica’ “Capítulo IV” follows “Capítulo III: La Anarquía Sónica”, issued by Oráculo Records on 27 September 2025, and the December 2025 single “Deadly Rhymes,” a 7″ pressed for Ombra Festival 2025 in a one-off run of 200 copies and drawn from the same forthcoming fourth chapter. No digital release date or additional preorder details beyond the shipping window have been announced. The preorder is one of four Oráculo Records vinyl releases opened this week, alongside IP307’s “IP307.1”, Frontmaschine’s “Rühren” and Post Analog Disorder’s “Burning The Edges.” About Estado De Bienestar Estado De Bienestar is a Spanish project led by Nico Cabañas, co-founder of Oráculo Records and the Ombra Festival. Cabañas launched the project following the closure of his earlier ventures Synths Versus Me and Almax und Forte, adopting a raw, analog-driven approach for the new material. The project’s debut, “La Escorpiona y Guateque Punk,” arrived in May 2025 via Oráculo Records as a limited double vinyl edition of 300 copies on orange and yellow 12″ records, also mastered by Daniel Hallhuber at Young and Cold Studios. That release was structured across two internal parts, “La Escorpiona” and “Guateque Punk,” and mixed EBM, industrial dub, darkwave, breakbeat and jazz elements. Side-Line reviewed the album, rating it 8 out of 10 and describing a record driven by “icy, minimalistic sounds, complemented by sparse vocals.” “Capítulo III: La Anarquía Sónica” followed on 27 September 2025, featuring a collaboration with Belgian synth artist Peter Bonne, recording as Chayell Zenn (Linear Movement, Twilight Ritual), who reworked his own track “The Enochian Keepers Of Time” into “Guardianes del Tiempo” for the album. The single “Deadly Rhymes” arrived in December 2025 as a preview of the fourth chapter, which Oráculo Records has now opened for preorder as “Capítulo IV: La Fiesta Seria y Nuevas Formas de Tecnaco.”

items.album: Klangstabil live review: ‘No Safe Distance’ at Markthalle Hamburg
items.excerpt: German electronic duo Klangstabil played Markthalle Hamburg on July 11, 2026, in a show presented by Living Dead Production. Karo Kratochwil, who interviewed the band about their live return earlier this year and previewed the Hamburg date in June, was in the room and filed this review. items.body: German electronic duo Klangstabil played Markthalle Hamburg on July 11, 2026, in a show presented by Living Dead Production. Karo Kratochwil, who interviewed the band about their live return earlier this year and previewed the Hamburg date in June, was in the room and filed this review. There are weekends when music forces you to declare your priorities. While The Cure were occupying Berlin’s Wuhlheide three nights in a row, I travelled farther north to see Klangstabil in Hamburg. This was not a judgement on which band mattered more. It was simply one of those decisions that had already been made somewhere below the level of reason. Some concerts are tempting possibilities. Others feel like places where you are supposed to be. Klangstabil are one of my favourite bands, although I do not see them live nearly as often as I would like. Perhaps that is partly why their concerts retain such force for me. Yet rarity alone cannot explain it. I have seen many beloved artists after long intervals without experiencing this particular loss of distance. With Klangstabil, it always happens. I cannot say precisely at which point. At first, I am still listening in the usual way: noticing the construction of the sound, the tension between its elements, the way a sequence develops or a vocal line enters. Then, somewhere along the way, that analytical position becomes impossible to maintain. I stop observing the concert from the outside and realise that the music has already found its way underneath whatever protection I brought into the room. This is one of Klangstabil’s strangest achievements. Their music is intelligent, sometimes extraordinarily so, but it never demands to be admired from a safe intellectual distance. Its formal precision is not there to demonstrate sophistication. It creates the conditions in which something much less orderly can be released. Their songs are full of pain, but pain is an easy material to mishandle. It can be aestheticised, exaggerated or made so attractive that it loses contact with the experience it supposedly represents. Klangstabil resist that temptation. Their sadness is shaped, certainly, but it is never made harmless. It retains the confusion and physical pressure of something that has actually been lived through. That honesty is not comfortable. Nor should it be. Klangstabil at Markthalle: the room and the material The Hamburg concert, presented by Living Dead Production at Markthalle on 11 July, carried exactly this emotional weight. Markthalle was a very good place for it. There is history in the room, but it does not impose itself on the performance. The venue is large enough to give the sound space and physical force, yet close enough for the musicians never to become remote figures trapped behind lights and equipment. That closeness mattered. Klangstabil’s concerts depend on contact. The familiar material did not feel preserved or ceremonially presented. There was no sense of being invited to admire a catalogue from the proper historical distance. The songs remained open, unsettled and capable of hurting in the present tense. They were not memories of emotions. They were emotions happening again. Boris May’s vocal performance stood at the centre of that experience. There are singers who represent pain convincingly and singers whose voices seem to carry its actual consequences. Boris belongs to the latter group. Even when the delivery is controlled, one hears the pressure beneath that control. The voice can sound restrained and close to breaking at the same time, as though each line has to pass through resistance before it can be released. Nothing about it feels like emotional exhibitionism. That distinction is important. He does not appear to expose himself in order to be watched. He gives the songs to the audience because the act of giving them seems necessary. This is why the performance feels addressed rather than merely delivered. Klangstabil do not seem to sing towards an anonymous mass of listeners. They sing to the people in front of them. The difference may sound small on paper, but inside a concert it changes everything. It removes the protective layer between performer and audience. Maurizio Blanco provides another kind of presence. His command of the electronic structure is exact, but the precision never becomes clinical. He holds the architecture together while allowing the emotional material inside it to remain unstable. When his voice joins Boris’s, it does not simply add another vocal layer. It changes the balance of the room. One voice carries exposure; the other gives it weight, contrast and a different human temperature. Together, they embody the tension that has always made Klangstabil so compelling: discipline and emotional excess existing not as opposites, but as conditions for one another. The music is controlled because what it contains is not. An audience that did not look away Yet the most affecting element of the Hamburg show was not located solely onstage. It existed in the movement between the band and the audience. The people in Markthalle were not passive recipients waiting for favourite moments to recognise and applaud. They listened with the concentration of people who understood what was being entrusted to them. The emotional force coming from the stage did not disappear into the room. It was received and returned. That exchange is difficult to describe without making it sound sentimental. It was not sentimental. It was intense, at moments almost painfully so, but there was nothing soft or vague about it. Klangstabil placed something raw in front of the audience, and the audience did not look away. I am often suspicious of describing concerts as cathartic. The word is used too easily, as though a few powerful songs could cleanse pain and send everyone home repaired. Klangstabil offer no such convenient transformation. Their music does not make difficult feelings disappear. It does something more honest: it allows them to exist openly for a while, without disguise and without isolation. The weight remains. What changes is that it is no longer carried alone. Perhaps this is why I repeatedly leave Klangstabil concerts shaken rather than simply impressed. I do not come away thinking only about the quality of the compositions or the power of the performance, although both are undeniable. I leave with the unsettling sense that something private has been recognised without having to be explained. That happened again in Hamburg. At some point, I stopped thinking about how I would later describe the concert. The part of me that normally records, compares and arranges impressions had gone quiet. There was only the sound, the two people producing it and the strange collective understanding forming in front of them. The show was beautiful, but beauty is not quite the right measure. Beauty can be observed without consequence. This could not. Klangstabil do not merely communicate emotion. They create the conditions in which emotional distance becomes difficult to maintain. They find the unguarded place, not through manipulation or theatrical excess, but through an honesty so concentrated that resistance begins to feel pointless. Some musical choices are not really choices between what is greater and what is smaller. They are choices between the event everyone is talking about and the one that feels personally necessary. On that July evening, thousands of people were gathered around The Cure in Berlin. I was standing inside Markthalle in Hamburg, watching Klangstabil remove the distance between themselves, their music and the people who had come to meet them there. For me, there was nowhere else to be. Review by Karo Kratochwil. About Klangstabil Klangstabil is the German electronic duo of Maurizio Blanco and Boris May, formed in 1994. The project began as private studio research rather than material intended for release, with the first vinyl following in 1995; more than a dozen records have appeared since, on vinyl, CD and successive digital formats. In 1998, the duo founded their own label, MHz Records, releasing their own work alongside artists spanning delicate electronics to grindcore. Klangstabil’s catalogue has moved from experimental sound collage and abstract electronics toward the emotionally direct electropop of recent releases, guided by what the band describes as its working method: “one step back, two steps forward.” After a seven-year absence from the stage, Klangstabil returned to live performance in 2026, a comeback Karo Kratochwil covered for Side-Line in an interview with the band. The July 11 Markthalle Hamburg date, presented by Living Dead Production, was part of that live return.

items.body: London label World of Echo will release “Fully Nowhere: A World Resources Archive” (WOE025) on double vinyl and digitally on August 7, 2026. The 25-track compilation draws on lathe-cut 7″ singles and LPs released by the New Zealand label World Resources, predominantly across the 1990s, and centers on the Wellington free noise trio Surface of the Earth and the musicians around them. World of Echo have shared two tracks ahead of release: “Winter Call” by Lucky Stars, Donald Smith’s noise pop project, and “Strontium” by Gorgecop, Paul Toohey’s project that launched World Resources. World Resources’ catalogue was small and released in miniscule editions, its lathe-cuts made by DIY vinyl manufacturer Peter King in the Southern Alps town of Geraldine and rarely circulating beyond a small group of collectors. Interest in the material grew after Surface of the Earth’s 1995 double LP was reissued on CD by Bruce Russell’s Corpus Hermeticum, then on Utech, and finally on vinyl by Black Editions. Paul Toohey’s K-Group project resurfaced in 2017, followed by a World Resources retrospective exhibition in Hastings, new recordings from Surface of the Earth, K-Group and Donald Smith’s Destrifan, K-Group live dates in Europe in 2019 and 2023, and a Surface of the Earth European tour in 2025. World of Echo hosted a K-Group instore during the 2023 European dates, where the plan for “Fully Nowhere” was made. ‘Fully Nowhere’ tracklist The compilation is arranged loosely chronologically across four vinyl sides. It opens with Gorgecop’s early singles, moves through Lucky Stars’ noise pop, and includes Tony McGurk’s solo project Sewer, excerpts from two New Zealand Guitar Orchestra free-noise recordings (“The Bad Shed” and “Skoda”), K-Group, a K-Group collaboration with New Zealand home-electronics artist Omit, and Surface of the Earth material spanning a 1990s “Shield” edit through to 2024 sessions recorded at Hastings Art Centre. It closes with a recent Destrifan piece. Side A: “Quapa-Extension”, “Slower Power”, “Squid”, “Strontium”, “K-Group”, “Section Across Europe” (Gorgecop); “Winter Call”, “Nuclear Famine” (Lucky Stars). Side B: “Rushlights”, “Watch Your Step” (Lucky Stars); “Smell of Man’s Room”, “Hospital” (Sewer); “The Bad Shed [Excerpt]”, “Skoda [Excerpt]” (New Zealand Guitar Orchestra); “Shield” (Surface of the Earth). Side C: “Commandcom”, “Visa 2” (Surface of the Earth); “Screen”, “Cars and the Soft Network” (K-Group); “Vacuum” (Sewer). Side D: “Decodes” (K-Group & Omit); “Fuel” (Sewer); “Programme+”, “2.2” (Surface of the Earth); “Sirens” (Destrifan). About Surface of the Earth and World Resources and World of Echo Surface of the Earth are a Wellington, New Zealand free noise trio of Donald Smith, Paul Toohey and Tony McGurk, whose slow-built guitar and electronic drones drove the World Resources label the three musicians ran through the 1990s. Toohey’s Gorgecop project issued the label’s first 7″ singles; reviewing them at the time, New Zealand fanzine de/create’s Nick Cain wrote that they sounded “fully nowhere”, the phrase that gives the new compilation its title. Toohey went on to record as K-Group, while Smith’s Lucky Stars project produced noise pop songs that circulated only in fragments via online compilations until now, and McGurk recorded as Sewer. World Resources’ recordings stayed largely unheard outside a small circle of collectors until Surface of the Earth’s 1995 double LP was reissued by Corpus Hermeticum, Utech and Black Editions, prompting the label’s gradual resurfacing from 2017 onward through new K-Group and Destrifan recordings, a Hastings retrospective exhibition, and European live dates by both K-Group and Surface of the Earth. “Fully Nowhere: A World Resources Archive” is the fullest document of that catalogue to date, released via World of Echo on August 7, 2026.

Noir Addiction ‘Pretty Things Don’t Last’: singles, lineup and credits The EP was previewed by two 2026 singles. “Serve Me Some Crime” arrived first
items.body: Italian industrial and alternative rock trio Noir Addiction release the six-track EP “Pretty Things Don’t Last” on 16 July 2026 through SoulPunx Records. Led by singer, guitarist and producer Sonny Lanegan, the EP follows a run of 2026 singles and lands on the Berlin label founded by Konstantin Dellos. Noir Addiction ‘Pretty Things Don’t Last’: singles, lineup and credits The EP was previewed by two 2026 singles. “Serve Me Some Crime” arrived first, on 20 March 2026, followed by “How She’s Got It” on 8 May 2026. Both singles came with videos directed and edited by Jack Lucas Laugeni and are available across digital platforms, including Spotify, Apple Music and Bandcamp. The band’s most recent single, “Money for the Honey”, followed on 19 June 2026 with its own video. “Pretty Things Don’t Last” was produced by Sonny Lanegan, engineered, mixed and mastered by Damiano Paoloni, and recorded at Sound Distillery in Italy. The lineup is Sonny Lanegan (vocals, guitars, synthesizers and programming), Nessie Zorba (keyboards and percussion) and Roberto Catanzaro (drums). Noir Addiction cite Nine Inch Nails, Depeche Mode and Gary Numan as reference points for their sound. Pretty Things Don't Last by NoirAddiction About Noir Addiction Noir Addiction is an Italy-based industrial rock and alternative rock project founded by Sonny Lanegan. Before Noir Addiction, Lanegan worked as a singer-songwriter for White Pulp and co-founded The Dead Good during a period based in Los Angeles; his music has appeared in television and film productions including “Mozart in the Jungle”, “Iron Fist” and “Z Nation”. The project’s public release timeline opened with the single “Chemical Bride” on 27 June 2025, followed by “Lust Of The Flesh” on 6 August 2025 and the 11-track album “Decadent Desire” on 9 September 2025. Side-Line reported in March 2026 that the previous lineup had split over a “difference in vision”, leaving Noir Addiction fronted by Lanegan with Nessie Zorba on keyboards and percussion and Roberto Catanzaro on drums. The 2026 singles “Serve Me Some Crime”, “How She’s Got It” and “Money for the Honey” precede the six-track EP “Pretty Things Don’t Last”, which SoulPunx Records – the Berlin label founded in 2017 by Konstantin Dellos – releases on 16 July 2026.

Why Pink Floyd’s ‘The Dark Side of the Moon’ gets a cassette
items.body: We Are Rewind will unveil a Pink Floyd edition of its WE-001 cassette player on July 16, 2026, paired with an exclusive cassette pressing of Pink Floyd’s “The Dark Side of the Moon.” The limited-edition set is priced at £159, €179 and $199 and follows We Are Rewind’s Duran Duran “Pop Trash” cassette player from December 2025 as the brand’s second artist-collaboration edition. Why Pink Floyd’s ‘The Dark Side of the Moon’ gets a cassette exclusive The cassette included in the set is described as a specially remastered pressing tied to the album’s 50th-anniversary campaign, which Side-Line covered in 2023 around its box-set reissue. Starscream Communications, handling press for the launch, states this cassette is exclusive to the We Are Rewind bundle and the only cassette version of that 50th-anniversary remaster. Pink Floyd drummer Nick Mason commented on the format: “I still have enormous affection for the cassette. It really was a major breakthrough – not only with the Sony Walkman but with some of the more up-market recorders. I still have my Nakamichi on the shelf and look forward to testing it with the new ‘The Dark Side of the Moon’ cassette.” We Are Rewind founder and CEO Romain Boudruche added: “To call ‘The Dark Side of the Moon’ a classic album is an understatement. In many ways, it set the tone for what an album experience should be as a continuous piece of sonic art but also used state-of-the-art production techniques and sounds which make it a true musical experience. We’re happy that We Are Rewind can play a part in helping preserve the physical album experience.” The player itself carries Bluetooth 5.1 connectivity, a rechargeable battery rated for up to 12 hours of playback, line-in recording for making mixtapes, and a frequency response of 30 Hz to 14,500 Hz (±3 dB). We Are Rewind cites cassette sales growth of 17.5% year on year in the US and 53% in the UK as context for the format’s continued run of releases. The set is available through retailers including Amazon, Rough Trade, Selfridges, Tower Records and Discogs, alongside We Are Rewind’s own site. About We Are Rewind We Are Rewind is a cassette-hardware brand best known for reviving the format with the WE-001 player, alongside the Curtis boombox and Freddie headphones. The company has built a run of artist-branded editions, starting with a Duran Duran “Pop Trash” cassette player and cassette in December 2025. The Pink Floyd “Dark Side Of The Moon” edition, unveiled July 16, 2026, is We Are Rewind’s second such collaboration.

items.body: Dead Can Dance released “The Cicadas” on July 15, 2026, exclusively through Bandcamp. The instrumental piece is the latest entry in the Dead Can Dance‘s ongoing series of Bandcamp-only monthly releases, following “Mon Amour Sauvage,” “Death Cults,” “Mnemosyne” and “Our Day Will Come” earlier this year. The Cicadas by Dead Can Dance Written by Brendan Perry, “The Cicadas” draws on Plato’s “Phaedrus” and the ancient Greek myth in which humans so enchanted by music that the Muses transformed them into eternal singers. Perry describes the piece as a reflection on music, wisdom and the pursuit of knowledge. The track was recorded and mixed at Temenos Studio in Greece. It features Perry alongside David Kuckhermann on bendir and riq, Yannis Pantazis on aulos, and the Rhodope Women’s Ensemble. “The Cicadas” is an instrumental piece and carries no separate video release. It is available now as a name-your-price digital download on Bandcamp. About Dead Can Dance Dead Can Dance formed in Melbourne, Australia, in 1981, founded by Brendan Perry and Lisa Gerrard. The duo relocated to London in 1982 and signed to 4AD, releasing a self-titled debut album in 1984. Across the following decade, the band built a catalogue that combined gothic rock, world music and neoclassical composition, including “Spleen and Ideal” (1985), “Within the Realm of a Dying Sun” (1987), “The Serpent’s Egg” (1988), “Aion” (1990), “Into the Labyrinth” (1993) and “Spiritchaser” (1996). The band disbanded in 1998 before reuniting for the album “Anastasis” in 2012 and touring intermittently in the years since, including the 2018 album “Dionysus.” Perry has continued to release music under the Dead Can Dance banner and through related projects. Side-Line has previously covered a solo single from bandmate Jules Maxwell featuring Polly Scattergood, and a live video of Lisa Gerrard and Maxwell performing “Noyalain (Burn)” from a 2022 concert recording. “The Cicadas” continues Dead Can Dance’s current run of standalone Bandcamp singles, released on a roughly monthly schedule through 2026.

items.body: Italian band Hot Sunday Blood released their single “Awakening” on June 30, 2026, through Black Hole Records. The track mixes alternative rock with industrial electronics and heavy guitar riffs, and arrives with an official video. “Awakening” is available now as a digital single and is streaming on Spotify. The song is credited to the band’s full line-up: Andrea Amerini on vocals, Stefano Capista on guitars, Paolo Iulita on bass and Carlo Borra on drums. About Hot Sunday Blood Hot Sunday Blood formed in Turin, Italy, in 2013. In its early stages the band’s sound drew on alternative rock with heavy rock influences, with each member bringing a different background, including metal, stoner, grunge, black metal, prog and new wave. The band describes itself as “plug and play,” reflecting an approach built around immediate, unrehearsed songwriting. Over time, the group’s sound shifted toward a more distinctive, electronics-inflected style, introducing industrial elements alongside Andrea Amerini’s vocals and Stefano Capista’s guitar riffs. Hot Sunday Blood has released three full-length albums and played more than one hundred live shows. In July 2018, the band opened for Doyle (of the Misfits) on the Turin date of his European tour. In May 2019, the band toured Romania, Croatia and Slovenia. It performed abroad again in 2023 at the Ostrava V Plamenech Festival and as a support act on the Farthest Outpost European tour. In 2024, Hot Sunday Blood played three rounds of the Emergenza Live festival in Turin, reaching the final at Hiroshima Mon Amour. In 2025, the band performed at the Balkan Metal Meeting in Bologna and abroad at Fajtfest in the Czech Republic and Balkan Metal Meeting in Hungary. “Awakening” is the band’s latest single release.

items.body: Mesh have announced a second leg of their “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” tour, adding seven European dates this autumn and confirming their first live appearance of 2027. The new run begins on August 30 at Electric Summer in Taunton, UK, before continuing through Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic. The announcement also confirms MESH for EASTSIDE Festival in Halle (Saale), Germany, on July 2, 2027, marking the band’s first announced show of next year. Fronted by vocalist Mark Hockings and guitarist, keyboardist and programmer Richard Silverthorn, Mesh continue to tour in support of “The Truth Doesn’t Matter,” the band’s latest studio album, released on March 27, 2026, via Dependent Records. The album reached number 15 in Germany and number 23 on the UK Download Chart. Ticket information for the new dates has not been announced. Mesh tour dates for 2026 and 2027 August 30, 2026 – Taunton, UK – Electric Summer October 1, 2026 – Krefeld, Germany – Kulturfabrik October 2, 2026 – Braunschweig, Germany – Westand October 3, 2026 – Dresden, Germany – Strasse E November 5, 2026 – Łódź, Poland – Scenografia November 6, 2026 – Halle (Saale), Germany – Capitol November 7, 2026 – Liberec, Czech Republic – Sever Synth Festival July 2, 2027 – Halle (Saale), Germany – EASTSIDE Festival About Mesh Mesh formed in Bristol, England, in 1991, when vocalist Mark Hockings and keyboardist Richard Silverthorn met at a concert. The duo built a catalogue of electronic alternative albums built around sequenced electronics, synth bass, guitars and Hockings’ vocals, releasing records including “The Point at Which It Falls Apart,” reissued in a 25th-anniversary edition in 2024. Hockings also records as Blackcarburning, a solo project whose singles and albums Side-Line has covered previously. Mesh’s 2026 album “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” arrived on Dependent Records on March 27, preceded by the singles “Exile,” “Hey Stranger” and “This World.” The band opened the album’s first tour leg shortly after release, and the newly announced second leg carries the “The Truth Doesn’t Matter” tour into its second year, alongside the band’s first confirmed festival date of 2027.
